title: Capacity Entropy Mitigation and SLO Recovery Checklist
author: Miguel Alvarez
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the concept of "capacity entropy" (slow divergence between provisioned resources, software configuration, and observed demand patterns), how to detect it, and an operational checklist to recover SLOs and protect error budgets. It is intended for SREs and on-call engineers supporting model-serving and routing services across Redwood (hosted, dedicated, private).

Context and motivation

- Capacity entropy arises from multiple small changes that individually appear harmless (policy tweaks, gradual tenant growth, quantization profile regressions, cache warming regressions) but collectively degrade SLOs over weeks.
- Left unchecked entropy eats error budgets and increases incident frequency. This doc provides detection signals, triage steps, mitigation actions, and post-incident review guidance focused on restoring steady-state with minimal customer impact.

Key definitions

1) Capacity entropy: measurable drift between expected capacity headroom and effective capacity delivered to traffic (cpu/gpu utilization, warm-pool ratios, request queueing, KV-cache hit rate).
2) SLO recovery window: operational target to recover a degraded SLO back to threshold within a bounded time (default 3 hours for P99 latency regressions; configurable per-service).
3) Entropy burst: a step change in entropy rate (e.g., sudden model rollout that increases per-token compute) that requires emergency remediation.

Detection signals (priority ordered)

- P99/P95 token latency increase sustained > 10% for 30m across at least two regions.
- Queue depth for serving workers > 2x baseline for 15m with steady input rate.
- Warm-pool occupancy < 60% for model hot-pool targeted to 95% (indicates churn).
- Global KV-cache hit rate drop > 15% compared to baseline for 1 hour.
- Autoscaler trigger rate (scale up events per hour) increases 3x baseline without corresponding traffic growth.
- Token-level cost per request increases > 12% with no billing anomaly.

Required telemetry and dashboards

- SLO dashboard (per-service): p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, saturation (GPU utilization), queue depth, warm-pool occupancy, KV-cache hit rate, autoscaler events.
- Entropy heatmap: 7-day rolling comparison of each metric vs baseline by region and model variant.
- Error-budget burn rate monitor with rolling 1h/6h/24h views and alerting thresholds.
- Synthetic canaries: latency and correctness probes exercising typical prompt lengths and embedding workloads.

Immediate on-call triage checklist (first 30 minutes)

1) Acknowledge and stamp incident channel; tag impacted service(s) and SLO dimension(s).
2) Correlate alerts with deployment events, config changes, model rollouts, or infra events in the past 2 hours.
3) Verify traffic levels (ingress tokens/sec) and rule out demand spike. If traffic spike, follow surge playbook; otherwise continue.
4) Check warm-pool occupancy and recent preemption/eviction logs. If warm-pool < 50%: scale temporary warm-pool by +30% and prioritize steadying (see Commands).
5) Check KV-cache hit rate and cache eviction logs. If hit rate dropped > 10%: enable prefix caching snapshot (see Mitigation Actions).
6) If autoscaler churn identified: temporarily pin num_workers to current steady-state and open compensating capacity request to Fleet (see Escalation).
7) If latency regressions align with a specific model variant: route a subset of traffic (10%) away from variant using routing policy to stable variant; increase canary traffic to validate fallback.
8) Declare SLO recovery window (default 3h) and log ETA in incident channel.

Mitigation actions (ordered by blast radius)

A. Low-blast (safe, quick)
- Increase warm-pool targets by 25% via runtime config: CLI: redwoodctl runtime set warm_pool.target --service <svc> --percent 125
- Enable conservative batching for affected route: redwoodctl route patch --route <r> --batch_policy conservative
- Temporarily increase autoscaler cooldown to reduce churn: redwoodctl autoscale update --svc <svc> --cooldown 300s
- Toggle KV-cache snapshot mode to restore hits: redwoodctl cache snapshot-restore --service <svc> --snapshot recent

B. Medium-blast (requires coordination)
- Rollback most recent model or quantization profile to last-known-good: runbook: Model Rollback Procedure (sections below).
- Reconfigure routing to steer high-cost traffic to cheaper or lower-latency model variant (policy-based routing).
- Add emergency warm GPUs from elastic-headroom pool: request via capacity-ops channel and attach to pool.

C. High-blast (emergency)
- Activate cross-region fallback for latency-sensitive routes and enable degraded feature mode (e.g., shorter context window for hosted API).
- Enact tenant-level throttles for non-SLA customers (via token priority queue) to preserve core SLOs.

Model Rollback Procedure (when model variant suspected)

1) Confirm variant-specific telemetry: per-variant latency, memory footprint, KV-cache behavior.
2) Create rollback plan with owner and target percent (start at 0 → 90% over 20 minutes).
3) Execute routing policy change: redwoodctl routing set-weight --service <svc> --variant-old 90 --variant-new 10; monitor P99 and error rate every 2 minutes.
4) Hold for 10 minutes; if metrics improve, continue ramp every 10 minutes. If metrics worsen, revert to previous routing and escalate to ModelOnboardingPager.

Capacity planning guardrails (preventive controls)

- Every model onboarding must provide: expected per-token GPU cycles, memory working set, KV-cache warmup profile, and synthetic runbook results. (Table: required onboarding outputs below.)
- Quarterly entropy scan: SRE runs automated comparison of headroom vs observed delivery across top-50 services; generate action items.
- Capacity shadowing: new models run at 0–5% shadow traffic for minimum 72h to observe real-world warming and cache behavior.
- Reserve an elastic-headroom pool equivalent to 10% of peak weekly GPU consumption for emergency absorption.

Onboarding requirements (one-time table - format as pipe-delimited)

| Field | Expected format | Acceptable range / notes |
| Model name | string | e.g., gpt-x-7B |
| Per-token GPU cycles | integer | provided as pGPUcycles; estimate with ±20% accuracy |
| Working set (GB) | decimal | memory footprint; must be < node_ram * 0.8 |
| Warm-pool target | percent | recommended 80–95% |
| KV-cache warmup time | minutes | measured using synthetic prompts |
| Canaries duration | hours | min 72h shadow; 24h for low-risk |

Escalation matrix and ownership

- Primary on-call: Service SRE (first 30m responsibility).
- Secondary: Platform Capacity (if warm-pool or autoscaler issues).
- Tertiary: Model Onboarding / Inference Performance team (if model variant implicated).
- Exec alert: if recovery window breached or error budget burn > 5x baseline in 24h, notify Head of SRE and Product.

Operational tooling and automations

- Entropy detector lambda: nightly job that computes week-over-week metric deltas and files tickets for >5% sustained drift across three metrics.
- Recovery Runbook generator: push-button in incident UI to create templated checklists and pre-fill commands for warm-pool scaling, route adjustments, and cache snapshot.
- Telemetry assertion suite: pre-commit and post-deploy checks that fail PRs when new model changes increase expected per-token cycles beyond threshold.

Post-incident review standards (what to capture)

- Incident timeline with exact timestamps for detection, mitigation actions (commands run), and recovery confirmation.
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence: include model commit id, quantization profile, infra events, and autoscaler logs.
- Capacity entropy delta report: 7d before vs 7d after across p99 latency, warm-pool occupancy, KV-cache hit, and GPU utilization.
- Corrective actions and owners with clear deadlines: configuration rollbacks, capacity increases, onboarding changes.
- Retro checklist: verification steps to prevent recurrence and a follow-up audit assigned to SRE or Performance.

Verification and closure criteria

- SLO metrics restored to < 5% above baseline for a full 24h window.
- Error-budget burn rate returned to normal cadence (< 1.5x baseline) for 24h.
- All corrective action items acknowledged and scheduled; no open P1 items.
- Postmortem published within 72 hours with links to evidence and follow-up tickets.

Appendix: example diagnostic commands and sample queries

- Check warm-pool occupancy:
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://ops.redwood/api/v1/warm-pool?service=<svc> | jq '.occupancy'
- Autoscaler event query (last 2h):
  rql "service=<svc> AND event in (scale_up, scale_down) AND timestamp > now()-2h" --format table
- KV-cache hit rate (PromQL):
  sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{service=\"<svc>\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{service=\"<svc>\"}[5m]))
